name: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
title: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
answer: Citation auditing and good law checking cover the verification of every authority cited in a brief, memo, opinion, or client advice, from case citations and pin cites to statutes, regulations, and secondary sources. Good law checking asks whether a cited case still supports the proposition after later rulings, amendments, repeals, or negative treatment such as overruling or distinguishing. The work sits in legal research and case strategy because a citation that is accurate but no longer good law can weaken an argument or expose counsel to sanctions. The site tracks 29 AI case law precedents, and each one can be checked for subsequent history as part of this discipline. It also applies to AI-generated drafts, where citations may be fabricated or misstated.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on primary sources and citators, including court websites, official reporters, and services such as Shepard's and KeyCite that flag negative treatment. Commercial research platforms like Westlaw, Lexis, and Bloomberg Law provide linked citations, dockets, and subsequent history, while free sources such as Google Scholar and court-run portals cover some of the same ground. The site tracks 732 AI tools, and some of those tools offer citation checking or citation extraction, though their output still needs verification against a citator or the primary source. A typical setup also includes a word processor, a PDF reader, and a citation manager to keep copies of the authorities checked. Access to dockets and court rules matters because good law checking often turns on a later order or a procedural change.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A citation audit starts by parsing each citation in the document and confirming that the cited source exists and that the quoted language and pin cite match the original. The auditor then runs the citation through a citator to see whether later cases have overruled, reversed, questioned, or distinguished it, and checks the subsequent history of the case. For statutes and regulations, the auditor checks for amendments, repeals, effective dates, and any pending legislation that could change the text. Where generative AI has produced a draft, the auditor treats every citation as unverified until it is matched to a primary source. The results are recorded in a memo or a table that lists the citation, the treatment found, the date checked, and the reviewer.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are professional and procedural: a court may sanction counsel for citing a fake, misquoted, or overruled authority, and a client may suffer from advice built on bad law. Provenance matters, so firms commonly keep a record of which citator was used, when the check was run, and who reviewed the result, because citator content changes over time. Confidentiality and privilege apply when client documents or draft briefs are uploaded to an AI tool, and the tool's terms and data retention practices become part of the risk review. The duty of candor to the tribunal and the duty of competence both point toward human review of any automated citation check, and the specific rules vary by jurisdiction.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Courts are increasingly aware of fabricated citations, and some have issued standing orders or local rules that require counsel to disclose the use of generative AI in drafting. Citators and research platforms are adding automated treatment summaries and citation validation, while drafting tools are beginning to check citations as text is entered. The likely direction is toward more continuous checking, where a citation is validated at the moment it is inserted and rechecked before filing. Standards for provenance and audit trails may become more common, so that a firm can show what was checked and when. The site tracks 6979 state AI bills, and enacted versions will add new statutory text to audit, which keeps good law checking a moving target.
